paragraphs.heading: Between liquid and solid
paragraphs.text: A liquid crystal is a state of matter whose properties fall between those of an ordinary liquid and a solid crystal. A molecule that can form these in-between phases is called a mesogen. Like a crystal, a liquid crystal has an inner order, and that order shapes its optical, electrical and magnetic properties. Yet it can also flow and react to outside stimuli the way a liquid does.

paragraphs.heading: Three main kinds
paragraphs.text: Liquid crystals fall into three main types. Thermotropic ones enter the liquid crystal phase as their temperature changes. Lyotropic ones depend on both temperature and how concentrated the molecules are in a solvent, usually water. Metallotropic ones contain both organic and inorganic molecules, and their change also depends on the ratio between the two. The first two types are made mostly of organic molecules, though a few minerals belong to them as well.

paragraphs.heading: Where they show up
paragraphs.text: Liquid crystals of the lyotropic kind are plentiful in living things: many proteins and cell membranes are liquid crystals, and so is the tobacco mosaic virus. Soap solutions, related detergents and some clays are examples from the mineral world. In technology, their mix of crystal-like order and liquid-like flow makes them useful in displays, sensors and soft robotics. Liquid-crystal displays, or LCDs, are in widespread use.

paragraphs.heading: Two melting points
paragraphs.text: The story starts in 1888, when the Austrian scientist Friedrich Reinitzer studied compounds derived from cholesterol. He found that one of them, cholesteryl benzoate, has two melting points. At 145.5 °C it turns into a cloudy liquid. Heat it to 178.5 °C and the cloudiness clears. He also found that it reflects circularly polarized light and can rotate the direction in which light is polarized.

paragraphs.heading: Lehmann takes over
paragraphs.text: Reinitzer did not keep working on the subject, but Otto Lehmann did, bringing skills in crystallography and microscopy. He studied the double-melting compounds in polarized light, using a microscope with a heated sample holder. The cloudy middle phase could clearly flow, yet what he saw under the microscope convinced him it was a solid. In 1904 Lehmann coined the name cholesteric liquid crystals.

paragraphs.heading: From curiosity to screens
paragraphs.text: For about 80 years, liquid crystals stayed a pure scientific curiosity. In 1962, RCA Laboratories began studying them for flat panel electronic displays. Richard Williams put an electric field across a thin layer of a type of liquid crystal called nematic, and saw a regular pattern form. This led his colleague George Heilmeier to work on a flat display to replace the cathode ray tube in televisions. But their material was only a liquid crystal above 116 °C, which made it impractical for a commercial display.
